lessons.title: Branching Logic with if, else if, and else
lessons.description: Make your code take different paths based on conditions — the foundation of decision-making in every program.

sections.heading: Why programs need to make decisions
paragraphs: Without branching, code always runs top-to-bottom with no variations. Branching lets you run specific code only when a condition is true — like showing an error message only when a form is empty, or granting access only when a user is logged in.

sections.heading: The basic if statement
paragraphs: An if statement checks a condition. If the condition is truthy, the code inside the braces runs. If it is falsy, the entire block is skipped.
list: The code to run goes inside curly braces: { ... }
If you only have one line, the braces are optional — but always use them for clarity

sections.heading: Adding else and else if
paragraphs: else provides a fallback path when the condition is false. else if lets you check additional conditions before reaching the final fallback. JavaScript evaluates them top-to-bottom and runs the first matching branch — then skips the rest.

codeExamples.heading: Basic if, else if, else
explanation: 28 is not greater than 30, so the first condition is false.
28 is greater than 20, so else if matches and prints "Nice weather!".
Once a branch matches, the remaining else if and else blocks are skipped.

codeExamples.heading: Nested conditions
explanation: The outer if checks hasTicket — it is true, so we enter that block.
Inside, a second if checks the age — 15 is under 18, so the inner else runs.
Nesting works, but too many levels make code hard to read. Consider combining conditions with && when possible.

practice.task: Write a function getGrade(score) that returns "A" for 90+, "B" for 80–89, "C" for 70–79, "D" for 60–69, and "F" below 60. Test it with 95, 72, and 55.
hints: Use else if for each grade band.
practice.note: Try passing negative numbers or values above 100 — what should your function do?

keyTakeaways: if runs code only when its condition is truthy; else provides a fallback.
else if lets you check multiple conditions — they are evaluated top to bottom.
Once a matching branch runs, all remaining branches are skipped.
Always use curly braces, even for single-line blocks, to avoid mistakes.
lessons.challenge: Write a function canRide(height, hasAdult) that returns true if the person is 48+ inches tall, OR if they are at least 36 inches and accompanied by an adult. Return false otherwise. Test it with height/adult combinations.

lessons.title: Truthy and Falsy Value Evaluation
lessons.description: Understand which values JavaScript treats as true and false — so you can write cleaner conditions without unnecessary comparisons.

sections.heading: Not everything is a boolean
paragraphs: JavaScript lets you use any value in an if condition, not just true or false. It automatically converts the value to a boolean behind the scenes using truthiness and falsiness rules.

sections.heading: The falsy values
paragraphs: There are exactly six values that JavaScript treats as false:

sections.heading: Everything else is truthy
paragraphs: Any value not in the list above is truthy. This includes "0" (a non-empty string), [] (empty array), {} (empty object), and -1 (negative numbers). Beginners often expect these to be falsy, but they are not.

sections.heading: Practical uses of truthiness
paragraphs: You can write shorter code by relying on truthiness instead of explicit comparisons. For example, if (name) is equivalent to if (name !== "") for a string variable. This pattern is cleaner and less error-prone.

codeExamples.heading: Truthy and falsy in action
explanation: The number 0 is falsy, but the string "0" is truthy — because it is a non-empty string.
Negative numbers like -1 are truthy — only 0 is falsy among numbers.
An empty array [] is truthy. This surprises many beginners.

codeExamples.heading: Practical defaults with truthiness
explanation: The || operator uses truthiness — an empty string is falsy, so it falls back to "Anonymous".
When score is 0, if (score) is false — be careful if 0 is a valid value you want to treat as present.
For numeric defaults where 0 is valid, use ?? (nullish coalescing) instead of ||.

practice.task: Without running the code, predict whether each condition is truthy or falsy: "false", [], {}", "0", NaN, -0. Then verify your answers in the console.
hints: "false" is a string — non-empty strings are truthy.
[] is an array — objects/arrays are always truthy.
NaN is one of the six falsy values.
practice.note: The gap between what you expect and what JavaScript does is where most truthiness bugs live.

keyTakeaways: Only six values are falsy: false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN.
Everything else is truthy — including "0", [], {}, and -1.
You can use truthiness directly in conditions: if (name) is cleaner than if (name !== "").
When 0 or "" are valid values, use ?? instead of || to avoid accidentally replacing them.
lessons.challenge: Write a function describe(value) that returns a string describing the input: "empty" if it's falsy, "zero" if it's the number 0, "string" if it's a non-empty string, "number" if it's a non-zero number, or "other" for everything else.

lessons.title: Compact Conditionals with the Ternary Operator (? :)
lessons.description: Replace simple if/else blocks with a one-line expression — the ternary operator makes short conditions concise and readable.

sections.heading: The ternary syntax
paragraphs: The ternary operator is a shorthand for if/else. It has three parts: a condition, a value to return if true, and a value to return if false. The syntax is: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse.

sections.heading: When to use it
paragraphs: The ternary is ideal for choosing between two values — like assigning a default, displaying different text, or selecting a CSS class. If your logic involves multiple statements or side effects, stick with a regular if/else block instead.

sections.heading: Nesting ternaries
paragraphs: You can chain ternaries for multiple conditions, but this gets hard to read quickly. As a rule: if you have more than one ternary, use if/else if instead. Keep ternaries short and simple.

codeExamples.heading: Basic ternary usage
explanation: The ternary does exactly the same thing as the if/else, but in one line.
The part before ? is the condition. The part between ? and : runs if true. The part after : runs if false.
Use ternaries when choosing between two values. Use if/else when running multiple statements.

codeExamples.heading: Ternary in template literals and functions
explanation: Ternaries work perfectly inside template literals — they keep the expression clean.
Returning a ternary from a function is a common pattern for simple two-outcome logic.
Both examples would be more verbose with if/else blocks.

practice.task: Rewrite this if/else using a ternary: let greeting; if (hour < 12) { greeting = "Good morning"; } else { greeting = "Good evening"; }. Then write a function getDiscount(price, isVIP) that returns 10% off for VIPs and 0 otherwise.
hints: The ternary: let greeting = hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : "Good evening";
Test with different price and VIP combinations.
practice.note: If you find yourself writing condition ? a : b ? c : d, stop — use if/else instead.

keyTakeaways: The ternary operator condition ? a : b is a compact replacement for simple if/else assignments.
Use it when choosing between two values, especially inside template literals and return statements.
Avoid nesting ternaries — if you need multiple branches, use if/else if instead.
Ternaries are expressions (they produce a value), while if/else is a statement (it runs code).
lessons.challenge: Write a function getTicketPrice(age, isStudent) that returns: $15 for adults (18+), $10 for students under 18, $8 for children (under 12), and free for seniors (65+). Use ternaries where it makes sense.

lessons.title: Multi-branch Conditionals with switch Statements
lessons.description: Choose between many possible values cleanly — switch statements handle multiple comparisons better than a long chain of if/else if.

sections.heading: When switch beats if/else
paragraphs: When you are comparing one variable against many specific values, a switch statement is cleaner than multiple else if blocks. It is especially useful for menu selections, command parsing, and handling different data types or status codes.

sections.heading: How switch works
paragraphs: A switch evaluates an expression once and compares it against each case value using strict equality (===). When a match is found, the code under that case runs. The break statement exits the switch — without it, execution "falls through" to the next case.
list: case value: — runs if the expression equals this value
default: — runs if no case matches (like else)

sections.heading: Fall-through: a feature and a trap
paragraphs: Without break, a matching case will continue executing into the next case. This is usually a bug, but occasionally useful — like when multiple cases should run the same code. Always include break unless you intentionally want fall-through.

codeExamples.heading: Basic switch statement
explanation: day is compared against each case using ===.
Saturday and Sunday share the same block — this is intentional fall-through (no break between them).
The default case catches anything not explicitly listed.

codeExamples.heading: Practical: HTTP status code handler
explanation: The function returns a message based on the HTTP status code — a classic use case for switch.
Using return instead of break exits both the switch and the function.
The default case handles unexpected status codes gracefully.

practice.task: Write a function describeAnimal(type) that uses switch to return: "Lion: fierce predator" for "lion", "Eagle: soaring bird" for "eagle", "Dolphin: intelligent swimmer" for "dolphin", and "Unknown animal" for anything else.
hints: Use switch (type) with a case for each animal.
Include break after each return (or use return directly).
practice.note: Try the same function with an object lookup — sometimes a simple object is better than switch.

keyTakeaways: Use switch when comparing one value against many specific cases — it is cleaner than long if/else chains.
Always include break after each case to prevent fall-through.
Group multiple cases together when they should run the same code.
The default case handles unmatched values — always include it for safety.
lessons.challenge: Write a getSeason(month) function using switch that returns "Spring" for 3–5, "Summer" for 6–8, "Autumn" for 9–11, and "Winter" for 12, 1, 2. Use intentional fall-through to group the months.

lessons.title: Catching Runtime Exceptions with try...catch...finally Blocks
lessons.description: Write code that gracefully handles errors instead of crashing — try, catch, and finally let you recover from unexpected problems.

sections.heading: What is a runtime exception?
paragraphs: An exception is an error that happens while your code is running — like trying to access a property on null, dividing by zero, or parsing invalid JSON. Without handling, these errors stop your program and show a red message in the console. try...catch lets you catch these errors and respond gracefully.

sections.heading: How try...catch works
paragraphs: Wrap risky code in a try block. If an error occurs, JavaScript jumps to the catch block instead of crashing. The caught error object contains information about what went wrong. You can also add a finally block that runs whether or not an error occurred — useful for cleanup.

sections.heading: When to use try...catch
list: Parsing user-provided JSON that might be malformed
Accessing properties on data from external APIs that might be missing
Reading files or making network requests that might fail
Running code that could throw based on unpredictable input

codeExamples.heading: Basic try...catch
explanation: JSON.parse("{invalid json}") throws a SyntaxError because the string is not valid JSON.
Without try/catch, this would crash the program. With it, the error is caught and handled.
The error.message property gives a human-readable description of the problem.

codeExamples.heading: try...catch...finally
explanation: throw new Error(...) creates an error manually — we will cover this in 1.6.6.
The finally block runs no matter what — whether the try succeeds, an error is caught, or an error is uncaught.
Finally is useful for cleanup: closing files, clearing timers, or resetting state.

practice.task: Write a function safeJSON(str) that tries to parse a JSON string and returns the result. If parsing fails, it should return null and log the error. Test with '{"name": "Vishnu"}' and '{bad json}'.
hints: In the catch block, log error.message and return null.
Don't forget: the try block should return the parsed result.
practice.note: Always log or report errors in catch blocks — swallowing errors silently makes debugging very hard.

keyTakeaways: try wraps code that might throw an error; catch handles the error gracefully.
The catch block receives an error object with .message and .name properties.
finally always runs — use it for cleanup code that must execute regardless of errors.
Use try/catch for operations that depend on external input (JSON parsing, API data, user files).
lessons.challenge: Write a function fetchUserData(jsonString) that parses a JSON string and accesses user.name. If the JSON is invalid OR the user property is missing, catch the error and return { name: "Guest" }. Test with valid JSON, invalid JSON, and JSON without a user property.

lessons.title: Throwing Explicit Exceptions using throw new Error()
lessons.description: Stop code execution deliberately when something is wrong — throwing errors makes your functions communicate problems clearly.

sections.heading: Why throw errors?
paragraphs: Sometimes a function receives invalid input or encounters an impossible state. Instead of returning a misleading result, you should throw an error immediately. This forces the caller to deal with the problem — either by handling it with try/catch or by passing valid input.

sections.heading: The throw statement
paragraphs: The throw statement stops the current function and creates an error. You can throw any value, but always throw Error objects — they include a stack trace that tells you where the error originated. The most common pattern is throw new Error("message").

sections.heading: Precondition checks
paragraphs: A great use of throw is validating function inputs at the top. Check that arguments are the right type, within range, or not null. This technique is called guarding and catches bugs early — before they cause mysterious problems downstream.

codeExamples.heading: Throwing errors for invalid input
explanation: The function checks its inputs before doing any work — this is called a precondition check.
If width or height is not a number, a clear error is thrown immediately.
If dimensions are negative, another specific error is thrown — the caller knows exactly what went wrong.

codeExamples.heading: Rethrowing errors
explanation: The function validates the input and throws specific, descriptive errors for each problem.
The catch block logs the error for debugging, then rethrows it so the caller can handle it too.
Rethrowing is important — logging an error doesn't fix it. The caller needs to know something went wrong.

practice.task: Write a function setUsername(name) that throws an error if the name is empty, if it's shorter than 3 characters, or if it contains spaces. Each case should have a different error message. Wrap your tests in try/catch.
practice.note: Make your error messages specific — "Invalid input" is less helpful than "Name must be at least 3 characters".

keyTakeaways: throw new Error("message") stops execution and creates an error with a descriptive message.
Always throw Error objects (not strings) so you get a stack trace for debugging.
Use precondition checks at the top of functions to catch invalid input early.
Use throw e to rethrow errors after logging — don't swallow errors silently.
lessons.challenge: Write a function transferMoney(from, to, amount) that validates: both accounts are objects, amount is a positive number, and the source account has enough balance. Throw specific errors for each validation failure. Return the updated balances as an object.
